core_summary: This chapter introduces the fundamental structural primitives of plane geometry—points, line segments, rays, and lines—and develops the concept of an angle as a quantitative measure of rotation turn expressed in degrees (°). Aligned with experiential learning, students construct angles using paper folding, clocks, compass roses, and protractors. The chapter establishes a full turn rotation as 360°, a straight angle (half turn) as 180°, and a right angle (quarter turn) as 90°. Angles are classified strictly by degree measure into acute (0° < θ < 90°), right (θ = 90°), obtuse (90° < θ < 180°), straight (θ = 180°), and reflex (180° < θ < 360°). Students master protractor alignment (matching vertex to center baseline and choosing the correct zero-scaling arm), paper-folding crease bisectors, perpendicular line formation, clock hand separations, Ashoka Chakra spoke angles (360° / 24 = 15°), and compass rose directional navigation. The chapter builds spatial reasoning essential for geometric proof and construction.
key_concepts: Geometric Primitives: A Point represents an exact location in space with zero dimensions. A Line Segment is the shortest straight path connecting two distinct endpoints, possessing a definite length. A Ray originates at an initial endpoint and extends infinitely in one direction. A Line extends infinitely in both opposite directions. Exactly one unique straight line passes through two distinct points.

Concept of an Angle as Angular Rotation: An angle is formed by two rays (arms) sharing a common endpoint (vertex). The magnitude of an angle measures the amount of rotation needed to sweep one arm onto the other, completely independent of the drawn physical length of the rays.

Degrees and Fractional Rotation Turns: Rotational turns are quantitatively measured in degrees (°). A complete 360° rotation forms a full turn; a 180° rotation forms a straight angle (1/2 turn); a 90° rotation forms a right angle (1/4 turn). Degree measure = Fraction of turn x 360°.

Angle Classification Taxonomy: Angles are categorized by measure: Acute Angles (0° < θ < 90°), Right Angles (θ = 90°), Obtuse Angles (90° < θ < 180°), Straight Angles (θ = 180°), and Reflex Angles (180° < θ < 360°).

Protractor Reading and Scale Selection: A protractor features an inner and outer degree scale from 0° to 180°. Accurate measurement requires aligning the protractor center point directly over the angle vertex, laying the baseline along one arm, and reading the degree mark on the scale that starts at 0° along that baseline arm.

Paper Folding and Perpendicular Lines: Folding a straight line crease directly onto itself creates an intersecting perpendicular crease meeting at four 90° right angles. Folding one angle arm onto another creates a precise angle bisector crease dividing the angle into two equal halves.

Clock Hand Angular Separations: A circular clock face is divided into 12 equal hour divisions, each spanning 30° (360° / 12). At H o'clock, the angle between minute and hour hands equals H x 30° (for H <= 6).

Ashoka Chakra and Spoke Angles: The Ashoka Chakra features 24 equally spaced spokes radiating from the central hub, dividing the 360° circle into 24 central angles measuring exactly 15° each (360° / 24).

Compass Rose and Navigational Angles: Cardinal directions (North, East, South, West) are separated by 90° right angles. Intercardinal directions (NE, SE, SW, NW) bisect these right angles into 45° acute angles.
Supplementary and Complementary Angle Relationships: Two angles are complementary if their sum equals 90°, and supplementary if their sum equals 180° (forming a linear pair on a straight line).
Reflex Angles and Explementary Rotation: Every interior angle θ (< 180°) has a corresponding exterior reflex angle measuring (360° - θ).
Intersecting Lines and Adjacent Angle Properties: When two straight lines intersect, opposite vertical angles are equal, and adjacent angles on a straight line sum to 180°.

key_terms.definition: A precise zero-dimensional location in space marked by a dot.
A straight path connecting two distinct endpoints, possessing a measurable length.
A straight line portion starting at a single fixed endpoint and extending endlessly in one direction.
A continuous one-dimensional straight path extending endlessly in both opposite directions.
The geometric figure formed by two rays sharing a common initial vertex, measured by rotation turn.
The common origin endpoint where two rays meet to form an angle.
An angle measuring exactly 90 degrees, representing a quarter rotation turn.
An angle whose degree measure is strictly greater than 0° and strictly less than 90°.
An angle whose degree measure is strictly greater than 90° and strictly less than 180°.
An angle measuring exactly 180 degrees, representing half a complete turn.
An angle measuring strictly greater than 180° and strictly less than 360°.
A semi-circular geometric tool calibrated from 0° to 180° used for measuring and drawing angles.

key_takeaways: Angle measure represents rotational turn sweep between arms and is entirely independent of arm length.
A full turn rotation equals 360°, a straight angle equals 180°, and a right angle equals 90°.
Angles are classified into acute (<90°), right (90°), obtuse (90°-180°), straight (180°), and reflex (180°-360°).
When measuring with a protractor, align the vertex to center baseline and follow the scale starting at 0° on the reference arm.
Folding a straight paper line crease onto itself forms a perpendicular line with four 90° right angles.
Each hour division on a clock face represents an angular rotation of 30° (360° / 12).
The 24 spokes of the Ashoka Chakra divide a circle into 24 equal 15° central angles.
Cardinal compass directions (N, E, S, W) are separated by 90°, while intercardinal directions (NE, SE, SW, NW) are separated by 45°.
The sum of adjacent angles on a straight line always equals 180°.
Subtracting an interior angle θ from 360° yields its corresponding reflex angle.
